question: In the lecture, a function \(f\) is defined as the limit of partial sums \(S_n(x)=\\sum_{j=1}^n f_j(x)\), and it is argued that \\(|f_j(x)|\\le m_j\\) for all \(x\) with \\(\\sum_{j=1}^\\infty m_j\\) convergent. Explain why the step \u201cchoose \(N\) so that \\(\\sum_{j=N+1}^\\infty m_j<\\epsilon\\)\u201d is enough to conclude that \(S_n\\to f\) uniformly (not just pointwise), and then state precisely what the uniform limit theorem lets you conclude about \(f\) given that each \(S_n\) is continuous.
answer:
Because \(\sum m_j\) converges, for any \(\epsilon>0\) there exists \(N\) such that the tail \(\sum_{j=N+1}^\infty m_j<\epsilon\). For any \(n\ge N\) and any \(x\),
\[
|f(x)-S_n(x)|=\left|\sum_{j=n+1}^\infty f_j(x)\right|\le \sum_{j=n+1}^\infty |f_j(x)|\le \sum_{j=n+1}^\infty m_j\le \sum_{j=N+1}^\infty m_j<\epsilon.
\]
The same \(N\) works for all \(x\), so the convergence is uniform. Since each \(S_n\) is a finite sum of continuous functions, each \(S_n\) is continuous; by the uniform limit theorem (uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous), \(f\) is continuous.
